transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-12-16
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Sophie (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Marcus (Aegis CTO), Priya (Head of MLOps), Samir (Infra)

00:00 Sophie: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick us off. quick intro, i'm Sophie with Redwood inference, and with me is Diego, our solutions engineer.
00:08 Marcus: Hi, Marcus here, thanks. Priya and Samir also on.
00:12 Diego: quick agenda, want to understand current infra, what workloads you want to run, isolation/compliance reqs, and scaling/burst expectations. we'll go over dedicated options and then define next steps. sound good?
00:26 Priya: Yep, sounds great. To start, we're evaluating whether we should go hosted vs dedicated vs private for inference. our primary concerns: data isolation, predictable latency, and cost predictability. we run several models - two production chat models and a reranker for search. peaks around payroll windows and EOD processing.
00:45 Sophie: perfect. can you share a little about traffic? QPS, token counts, and whether you need multi-tenant separation?
00:53 Priya: baseline is about 150 qps across models, peaks up to 1,200 qps for short windows maybe 5-10 minutes during eod. average prompt size is 120 tokens, responses around 80 tokens. we need dedicated capacity because of compliance: we can't have tenant co-mingling for certain payloads. also need audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
01:18 Diego: makes sense. dedicated is typically good for that — reserved GPU pools provide isolation and dedicated network boundaries, and you can keep logs and KMS in your VPC. are you considering private (on-prem) or VPC-private in cloud?
01:28 Marcus: prefer VPC-private on AWS in our account. compliance wants data not to leave our VPC and KMS keys we control.
01:36 Diego: good — Redwood Private supports customer-managed VPC peering and ability to bring your own KMS. for Dedicated hosted in Redwood-managed cloud we also offer VPC peering and dedicated subnets with private control plane options. small difference is on-prem vs our dedicated hosting for patching and SLA.
01:54 Samir: on peering, we need details around IP ranges, NAT, and if there are egress rules. also curious about bandwidth limits — during bursts we might have spikes.
02:05 Sophie: we'll share network architecture docs and the peering checklist. Diego — do you want to speak to burst allocation?
02:12 Diego: sure. There are two patterns we suggest: 1) headroom reserved — reserve extra GPUs in the Dedicated pool for scheduled bursts (e.g., payroll windows) so capacity is always there, or 2) burst-to-shared — try to allow short bursts to Redwood-hosted pools if policy allows. both have tradeoffs: reserved headroom costs more but guarantees capacity; burst-to-shared is cheaper but may have a fallback risk if neighboring capacity is constrained.
02:40 Priya: we can't use shared pools for sensitive workloads, so reserved headroom is more realistic. how do you size the headroom?
02:48 Diego: we use peak QPS and model costs (tokens/sec and GPU throughput). with your numbers — 1,200 qps short peak — we can map to GPU capacity based on model flop/profile. typically we propose a baseline reserved pool sized for average QPS with a headroom buffer for peaks. we can run benchmarks to map your exact throughput per GPU.
03:07 Priya: yes, we'll need benchmark numbers. also, how does autoscaling work? can you scale in under-provisioned mode and have a warm cache?
03:16 Diego: Dedicated supports autoscaling policies on the pool. scale-out latency depends on provisioning speed — if you have reserved headroom it's instant. for scale-from-zero it's constrained by instance spin up time. we also support KV/prefix caching to warm model state for faster cold-starts, and continuous batching to improve GPU utilization.
03:36 Marcus: what are your typical p95/p99 latencies for chat models on dedicated nodes?
03:42 Diego: rough ballpark depending on model size and quantization: p50 could be single-digit ms up to low hundreds for smaller models; p95/p99 vary more. that's why we recommend a benchmark — we'll provide sample p50/p95/p99 from our verified models and then run your model to calibrate.
04:00 Priya: ok. on security — SOC2, ISO, audit logs, SAML SSO, RBAC, and KMS. can you confirm Redwood Dedicated supports these?
04:09 Sophie: yes — we have SOC2 Type II, ISO documentation, SAML SSO, RBAC in the console, and integrations for forwarding audit logs. for KMS we support BYOK with customer-managed keys in VPC/private deployment. we'll attach the compliance pack.
04:23 Samir: what about data retention and model input persistence? we need to ensure PII isn't stored outside our control.
04:30 Sophie: dedicated/private gives you options — we can configure zero retention for inputs, or keep logs only in your SIEM. if you need absolute assurance, Private (on-prem or VPC with customer-managed control plane) is the safest.
04:42 Marcus: good. on pricing, how do you charge for Dedicated? fixed monthly for reserved GPUs plus optional burst and data egress?
04:52 Sophie: correct — reserved capacity is monthly commit for GPU pools, with options for burst credits or on-demand bursts. additional fees for data egress and advanced observability add-ons. we'll send a SKUized pricing sheet.
05:03 Priya: how do model updates and rollouts work? we have frequent model retrains and need quick rollouts without impacting latency SLOs.
05:12 Diego: Dedicated supports pinned model versions, canary and A/B rollout controls, and automatic fallback to a stable variant. rolling updates can be staged on a subset of the pool to reduce risk.
05:24 Marcus: for benchmark scope — what inputs do you need from us to size pools?
05:29 Diego: ideally: list of models (architecture/size), average and peak QPS per model, typical token length, acceptable latency targets (p50/p95/p99), and any constraints on co-mingling or data residency. with that we can run a synthetic workload test or a short PoC to validate.
05:46 Priya: we'll compile that. one more — do you support GPU quantization profiles / fp16 or int8? we've seen cost benefits with int8 but worried about quality.
05:55 Diego: yes, Redwood Optimize recommends quantization profiles per model and workload. we provide guidance and QC checks to ensure output quality remains acceptable. for sensitive models you can keep fp16 or full precision.
06:05 Samir: what's the SLA for Dedicated?
06:08 Sophie: SLA for Dedicated is 99.9% uptime for the serving pool, with latency objectives per pool that's configurable. we'll include SLA language in the contract docs.
06:16 Marcus: competitors — we were also looking at Vertex AI and Anthropic endpoint options. are there major differences?
06:24 Sophie: Vertex is fully cloud-native with deep GCP integration; Anthropic offers managed models. Redwood differentiates by providing a consistent runtime across hosted, dedicated, and private with heavy ops tooling for batching, cache, and rollout controls — better for teams that want control and predictable economics.
06:38 Priya: okay. sounds promising. next steps?
06:42 Sophie: recap: we'll send pricing SKU, compliance pack (SOC2/ISO), network peering checklist, and Diego will draft a benchmark plan. Marcus/Priya will share model list and traffic patterns. then we'll schedule a technical deep dive next week to align on PoC scope.
06:57 Marcus: agreed. thanks everyone.
07:00 Sophie: thanks, bye.

Notes on transcript quality: minor transcription noise, some product names slightly garbled in places (e.g., 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'k v cache'), occasional run-on lines and filler words preserved.
questions: What is the expected burst pattern and how should headroom be sized?
Can Redwood support customer-managed KMS and VPC-private deployment?
What are sample p50/p95/p99 latencies for our models on Dedicated?
